title: Continuous GPS updates enable profiling and linkage of the child over time
description: Regular transmission of live GPS coordinates creates a longitudinal location trail that can be linked to the same child and analyzed for recurring patterns such as home, school, routines, habits, and social relationships. Even if the flow's primary purpose is location reporting, the granularity and frequency of the data materially increase the ability to profile the child.
assumptions: The backend can associate successive GPS updates with the same child account, device, or session.

title: Live GPS coordinates directly identify the child's whereabouts
description: Precise, real-time GPS coordinates can identify the child by revealing their exact or near-exact current location. When tied to an account, device identifier, or parent-child relationship in the service, the flow enables singling out and identifying the child in the physical world.
assumptions: The backend stores or can access identifiers linking coordinates to a specific child or household.
uncertainty_note: Tree node citation is based on general LINDDUN identifiability structure; exact sub-node may vary by threat-tree version.

title: Real-time location tracking allows detection of the child's presence and activities
description: By receiving live GPS coordinates at regular intervals, the backend can determine whether the child is at home, school, a clinic, a place of worship, or other sensitive venues, and infer movement, attendance, and daily activities. This makes the child's behavior and presence detectable beyond what may be strictly necessary for basic service operation.
assumptions: The backend retains or processes timestamps and coordinates with sufficient precision to infer visits and movement.
uncertainty_note: Exact D threat-tree sub-node may differ across LINDDUN Pro versions; the threat applicability is high even if the node id is approximate.

title: High-frequency live location collection may exceed what is necessary
description: Collecting and transmitting precise GPS coordinates at regular intervals can expose more personal data than needed if the service could function with less frequent updates, coarser location, event-based reporting, or on-device processing. The flow therefore risks excessive disclosure through unnecessary granularity and continuous collection.
assumptions: The system's core functionality does not strictly require continuous high-precision tracking at the configured interval.

title: Child may be unaware of ongoing sharing of live location data
description: Because the child device continuously sends GPS coordinates to the backend, the child may not understand that their live location is being shared persistently, how often it is sent, or what inferences can be drawn from it. This is especially salient because the data subject is a child and may have limited capacity to understand the privacy implications.
assumptions: The interface does not provide age-appropriate, persistent, and comprehensible notice about continuous location sharing.

title: Continuous child-location processing may lack privacy-specific risk management
description: Processing live GPS data of a child at regular intervals is high risk and may require heightened privacy governance, including necessity/proportionality assessment, child-specific safeguards, retention limits, and security controls. If these are not explicitly managed, the flow creates a non-compliance risk due to insufficient privacy-aware cybersecurity and risk management.
assumptions: The system processes children's precise location data without documented child-specific risk assessment or equivalent controls.
uncertainty_note: This is a governance/compliance threat inferred from the nature of the flow; applicability depends on the organization's actual risk-management practices.

title: Location history stored without user-configurable retention or consent preferences
description: The backend writes each location ping into the Location History Store, which can create a privacy threat if users cannot set or change preferences for whether location history is stored, at what granularity, or for how long. This represents lack of data subject control over storage of highly sensitive location data.
assumptions: Assumes the system stores identifiable or reasonably linkable location history and does not provide effective user controls for storage/retention preferences.
uncertainty_note: Applies if user preference or consent controls for location-history storage are absent or ineffective; the flow description alone does not confirm whether such controls exist.

title: Centralized storage of detailed location pings increases exposure of sensitive movement history
description: Writing every location ping to a persistent Location History Store concentrates sensitive personal data about movements, routines, and places visited. If the store is accessible to more parties than necessary, reused broadly, or otherwise insufficiently scoped, the amount and sensitivity of exposed data can lead to excessive disclosure.
assumptions: Assumes the stored location pings are tied to a user, device, or account and retained in a form usable by internal or external parties.
uncertainty_note: Dd.4 is a good fit for excessive exposure to involved parties, but the flow description does not specify actual recipients or access scope beyond storage.

title: Storing continuous location history without privacy-focused risk management may violate obligations
description: Persistently storing each location ping creates elevated privacy risk due to the sensitivity and longitudinal nature of location history. If privacy-specific cybersecurity risk management is insufficient—for example around retention limits, minimization, access governance, and protection of the store—the processing may become non-compliant with applicable privacy requirements.
assumptions: Assumes applicable legal or policy obligations exist for sensitive location data and that risk management controls may be incomplete.
uncertainty_note: This is a non-compliance risk contingent on the governing legal/policy context and actual controls, which are not provided in the flow description.

title: Location pings may be unnecessarily analyzed or enriched during geofence evaluation
description: The Geofencing & Alert Engine receives raw location pings and may perform additional treatment, analysis, or enrichment beyond what is necessary to determine zone entry/exit, such as deriving movement patterns, frequent places, or behavioral inferences. This would disclose more about the data subject than needed for the stated purpose of geofence checking.
assumptions: Assumes the engine or downstream logic can retain or enrich incoming pings beyond a transient point-in-zone calculation.

title: Users may lack effective control over geofence processing of their location pings
description: If the backend forwards new location pings automatically to the Geofencing & Alert Engine without a granular preference or consent mechanism, data subjects may be unable to control whether their location is processed for zone entry/exit detection. This creates a lack of intervenability over a sensitive processing activity.
assumptions: Assumes the system does not provide a specific opt-in/opt-out or per-feature preference for geofencing-related location processing.
uncertainty_note: Applicability depends on whether user-facing controls for geofencing exist; the flow description alone does not confirm their absence.

title: Users may be unaware that backend location pings are forwarded for geofence evaluation
description: A data subject may not realize that location pings sent to the backend are subsequently forwarded to a separate Geofencing & Alert Engine for continuous zone entry/exit analysis. This secondary processing can be non-obvious, especially if the app only generally mentions location collection.
assumptions: Assumes notices are incomplete, overly generic, or do not clearly explain this internal forwarding and purpose.
uncertainty_note: This is a common risk for internal secondary processing, but actual applicability depends on the transparency notices presented to users.

title: Insufficient privacy-aware risk management for sensitive location transfer to geofencing engine
description: Forwarding precise or frequent location pings from the backend to a dedicated geofencing component introduces elevated privacy risk due to the sensitivity of location data and the possibility of continuous monitoring. If privacy-specific risk management is insufficient, the system may fail to assess necessity, proportionality, retention, access restrictions, and misuse scenarios for this transfer.
assumptions: Assumes no adequate privacy risk assessment or governance specifically covers this internal location-processing flow.
uncertainty_note: Non-compliance threats are partly organizational and cannot be confirmed from the flow alone; included because location processing typically requires explicit privacy risk management.

title: Zone definitions act as direct identifiers of a child's household and routine
description: The geofencing engine reads named locations such as home, school, and friend's house from the family account store. These location labels and associated coordinates can uniquely point to a specific child or family, because home and school together strongly narrow identity and household membership.
assumptions: Assumes zone definitions include precise coordinates and human-meaningful labels tied to a specific family account or child profile.

title: Combination of home, school, and friend locations makes the child distinguishable
description: Even if explicit names are absent, the set of configured geofence locations can create a very small anonymity set. A unique combination of home address, school, and regularly visited friend's house can single out one child from others.
assumptions: Assumes the engine can access multiple zone definitions together for one child or family and that these locations are sufficiently specific.

title: Sensitive private life details are disclosed through stored and processed zone definitions
description: Reading configured zones such as home, school, and friend's house reveals intimate aspects of the child's private life, including residence, education, social relationships, and habitual places. This exposes more than operational geofence data and can reveal sensitive context about the family.
assumptions: Assumes LINDDUN disclosure applies to inference or access to personal locations and relationships from the zone data.
uncertainty_note: Tree node citation is based on general LINDDUN disclosure categorization; the retrieved context did not include a disclosure subtree, so the exact node id may be approximate.

title: Zone definitions enable linkage of multiple events and profiles to the same child/family
description: Because the geofencing engine uses persistent configured zones from the family account store, subsequent location events and alerts can be linked back to the same child or family profile over time. This supports reconstruction of routines and cross-event correlation.
assumptions: Assumes persistent account- or child-specific zone records are reused across sessions and alerts.
uncertainty_note: Exact linkage subtree node may vary in LINDDUN Pro; retrieved context did not include linkage nodes, so this node id is best-effort.

title: Geofence alerts reveal the child's presence at a sensitive location or event
description: An arrival/departure notification is a system response that reveals that the child has entered or exited a defined zone at a particular time. This can expose the existence of an item of interest such as attendance at home, school, a clinic, a place of worship, or another sensitive venue.
assumptions: The notification content or timing is specific enough for the parent to infer the child's presence in the monitored zone.

title: Alert notifications may disclose more location information than necessary to the recipient
description: Pushing geofence notifications to the parent exposes personal location-event data outside the geofencing engine. If alerts include precise timestamps, zone names, repeated event history, or are sent to multiple parent accounts/devices, the flow may disclose more personal data than is necessary for the purpose of notifying about entry/exit.
assumptions: The system may include detailed metadata in the alert or distribute alerts to several devices/accounts associated with the parent.

title: Repeated geofence alerts enable profiling of the child's routines
description: A sequence of arrival/departure notifications can be analyzed to infer recurring patterns such as school schedule, home presence, extracurricular activities, religious attendance, or medical visits. This links multiple events to build a profile of the child's behavior and habits.
assumptions: Alerts are retained, observable over time, or otherwise available for analysis by the recipient or connected systems.

title: Child may lack effective control or awareness over geofence-triggered notifications to the parent
description: The flow sends location-event notifications to the parent automatically when zones are crossed. The child, as data subject, may be unaware of when alerts are generated or may have no ability to influence preferences governing which zones trigger alerts, how detailed they are, or when monitoring is active.
assumptions: The child is a relevant data subject and the system does not provide age-appropriate notice or controls over geofence monitoring behavior.
uncertainty_note: This is grounded in the child as data subject rather than the parent recipient; applicability depends on product governance and whether child-facing transparency/controls exist.

title: Geofence alerting may be non-compliant if notifications exceed the stated purpose or lawful basis
description: Sending arrival/departure alerts about a child to a parent can create regulatory risk if the processing lacks an appropriate lawful basis, adequate transparency, purpose limitation, data minimization, or age-appropriate safeguards. The risk increases when zones correspond to sensitive contexts or alerts are overly detailed or retained beyond necessity.
assumptions: Applicable privacy regulation imposes duties around transparency, minimization, lawful basis, and children's data.
uncertainty_note: Generic non-compliance is necessarily context-dependent because the exact jurisdiction, notices, consent model, and retention practices are not provided.

title: Parent may be unaware of the full privacy implications of submitting child profile and geofence data
description: During registration and setup, the parent provides the child's name, date of birth, school, and geofence zones. If the backend does not clearly explain what data is collected, why it is needed, how geofence data will be used, who can access it, and how long it will be retained, the parent may share highly sensitive child-related data without sufficient awareness.
assumptions: The flow includes collection of child identity, school, and location-related preference data at account creation time.

title: Parent may lack meaningful control over privacy preferences and consent for child-related data processing
description: The backend may collect and process child profile attributes and geofence definitions without offering granular choices about optional fields, geofence-related processing, notifications, sharing, or retention preferences. This creates a lack of control over how the child's personal data is processed.
assumptions: The service may not provide granular privacy settings or consent choices during onboarding.

title: Parent may be unable to rectify or erase child profile and geofence data after submission
description: Once the parent submits the child's profile and geofence zones to the backend, the system may not provide adequate means to correct inaccurate profile data, update school information, remove obsolete geofences, or delete the child's data entirely. This reduces data subject control over ongoing processing.
assumptions: The backend stores the submitted data beyond the immediate transaction and may not expose effective edit/delete mechanisms.

title: Collection of child profile and geofence data may create regulatory noncompliance risk
description: This flow processes personal data about a child, including identity attributes, school information, and location-related geofence zones. If the backend lacks appropriate transparency, parental authorization handling, lawful basis documentation, retention limits, or child-specific safeguards, the processing may violate applicable child privacy and data protection requirements.
assumptions: Applicable law imposes heightened obligations for children's data and location-related data.
uncertainty_note: Regulatory applicability depends on jurisdiction and the product's exact legal basis and notices.

title: Storage of directly identifying family and child profile data
description: The backend stores account and child profile data in the Family Account & Permissions Store in identified form, enabling direct association of records with a specific parent/family and child. This creates an identifying threat because the datastore processes personal data tied to known identities rather than minimizing or separating identifiers.
assumptions: Assumes account records and child profiles contain direct identifiers or stable account identifiers that can be linked to real individuals.

title: Storage of sensitive geofence zone data may exceed necessity
description: Geofence zone data associated with child profiles can reveal sensitive habits, home/school locations, and routines. If the store retains precise zone definitions or location-related metadata beyond what is strictly needed for the service, unnecessary sensitive data types are being processed, increasing disclosure impact.
assumptions: Assumes geofence zones include precise or semantically sensitive locations such as home, school, or other recurring places.
uncertainty_note: Applicability depends on whether all stored geofence attributes are strictly necessary for the feature and how precise the stored zones are.

title: Excessive retained volume of family, child, and geofence data
description: Combining account data, child profiles, permissions, and geofence zone data in one store may result in a larger volume of personal data than necessary for a single processing purpose. Retaining historical, duplicate, or overly granular records increases the amount of personal data exposed if accessed or reused.
assumptions: Assumes the datastore may keep multiple profiles, historical geofence changes, or detailed metadata rather than only the minimum current state.
uncertainty_note: The flow description does not specify retention limits or schema granularity, so this is a plausible minimization risk rather than a confirmed issue.

title: Child data subjects may be unaware of backend storage and processing
description: Child profile and geofence data are stored by the backend in a family account datastore, but the child data subject may not be aware that their personal and location-related data is being stored and managed in this backend system. This creates an unawareness risk regarding storage and processing of their personal data.
assumptions: Assumes children are data subjects and are not directly informed in an age-appropriate way about backend storage and processing.
uncertainty_note: This depends on the product's notice and transparency mechanisms; the flow alone cannot confirm whether adequate notice is provided.

title: Parent user may be unaware of the extent of data stored when configuring family features
description: A parent or guardian using the app may share child profile and geofence information through family-account features without fully understanding the extent, persistence, or downstream use of the stored data. This creates unawareness for the user sharing personal data on behalf of others.
assumptions: Assumes the app UX does not clearly explain what account, child profile, and geofence data are stored and for how long.
uncertainty_note: This is contingent on the transparency of the mobile app and backend notices; not directly observable from the flow alone.

title: Processing of identified location data for parent lookup
description: The backend processes a parent's request for a specific child's current location or location history, which inherently involves identified personal data because the location information is tied to a particular child/account relationship. This creates an identifying threat if the system processes directly identifiable child location records without sufficient minimization or separation.
assumptions: Assumes the request includes or is linked to a specific child identity/account and that the backend can directly retrieve that child's location/history.

title: Child may be unaware that location/history is disclosed in response to parent requests
description: When the backend serves parent requests for a child's current location or historical movements, the child as data subject may not be aware of the collection, processing, or disclosure of their location data for this purpose. This is especially relevant for historical location access, which can reveal sensitive movement patterns.
assumptions: Assumes the child is the data subject and the system does not provide clear, timely notice about parent-initiated access to current or historical location data.

title: Child may lack preference or consent controls over parent access to location data
description: The backend may provide location or location-history data to the parent without allowing the child, as data subject, to set preferences or exercise meaningful control over whether current location, historical location, or retention-based access is enabled. This reflects lack of intervenability and preference control over sensitive personal data processing.
assumptions: Assumes the product supports parent access by default or with limited child-configurable controls, and that the child is entitled to some degree of preference/consent control in the deployment context.
uncertainty_note: Applicability depends on the child's age, legal role, and product policy; in some parental-control contexts the child may not be granted direct control.

title: Backend access may over-expose detailed location history to parties beyond strict need
description: This flow transfers stored location history from the data store to the backend so it can serve a parent's map/history view. Detailed historical location traces are highly sensitive and can reveal routines, home/school addresses, and other intimate patterns. If the backend retrieves broader history than necessary, or makes it accessible to internal services, operators, or downstream recipients beyond the intended parent-facing function, the flow creates a data disclosure risk through excessive exposure.
assumptions: Assumes the backend can access raw or fine-grained location history and that access controls, minimization, or purpose limitation may be insufficiently enforced for this retrieval.

title: Retrieved location-history attributes can act as quasi-identifiers enabling linkage
description: Location history commonly contains timestamps, recurring places, and movement patterns that can uniquely distinguish an individual. When the backend retrieves and processes this history, those attributes can be combined to link records belonging to the same child or household, or correlated with other backend-held datasets, increasing linkability beyond the original storage purpose.
assumptions: Assumes the backend holds or can access additional attributes or datasets that make correlation feasible.

title: Serving historical views may incentivize retaining location history longer than necessary
description: Because the backend retrieves stored location history to provide a history view, the system may retain historical location data for extended periods to support this feature. If retention is not bounded to what is necessary for the stated purpose, this flow contributes to violation of the storage limitation principle.
assumptions: Assumes the feature does not enforce a clearly justified retention window or deletion policy aligned with necessity.
uncertainty_note: This threat is grounded in the existence of a history-serving flow, but the actual retention-policy violation depends on system policy details not provided.

title: Data subjects may lack effective control over retrieval and use of their location history
description: The backend's retrieval of stored location history for a parent's history view may occur without granular controls for the tracked individual or account holder to limit what period, precision, or categories of location data are used. This creates a risk that data subjects are unable to set preferences or intervene in how their historical location data is processed and displayed.
assumptions: Assumes the system lacks granular privacy controls such as disabling history, limiting precision, or restricting visible time ranges.
uncertainty_note: The cited node concerns preferences/control; applicability depends on whether such controls are absent in the implemented product.

title: Secondary guardian may be invited without sufficient awareness of what child location data access is being granted
description: When the parent submits an invitation for a secondary guardian, the backend may process the request without ensuring the inviting user is clearly informed about the scope of sharing, such as continuous location visibility, historical access, or duration of access. This can lead to personal data about the child being shared more broadly than the parent intended.
assumptions: The invitation flow may not clearly communicate the exact data categories, duration, and consequences of granting access to the secondary guardian.

title: Insufficient control over sharing preferences for invited secondary guardians
description: The backend may support sending an invitation without offering granular controls over the invited guardian's permissions, such as limiting access duration, restricting precise versus coarse location, or revoking pending/accepted access easily. This reduces the data subject's or responsible parent's ability to control how the child's personal data is processed.
assumptions: The system allows inviting additional viewers but may not provide fine-grained preference settings or easy revocation tied to this flow.

title: Invitation flow may disclose more child-related personal data than necessary to the secondary guardian
description: If the backend packages or enables access beyond what is necessary for the invitation purpose, the invited secondary guardian could receive excessive personal data, such as precise live location, historical movement, profile details, or related metadata, instead of the minimum needed to establish access. This constitutes unnecessary disclosure in the sharing workflow.
assumptions: The invitation or subsequent access provisioning may expose more data than minimally necessary for adding a secondary guardian.
uncertainty_note: The cited node Dd.3.1 is about unnecessary further treatment/enrichment; it is used here approximately to capture over-broad processing/disclosure during provisioning because the retrieved context is limited.

title: Sharing child location with additional guardians without privacy-focused risk management may create compliance gaps
description: Adding a secondary guardian expands the set of recipients for sensitive child location data. If the backend implements this sharing flow without documented privacy risk assessment, safeguards for child data, recipient verification, retention limits, and auditable consent/authorization handling, the system may fail to meet applicable legal and organizational privacy obligations.
assumptions: Child location data is sensitive and subject to heightened compliance expectations; the invitation flow may not have been designed with explicit privacy risk management controls.

title: Child live location disclosed to a predetermined secondary guardian
description: The backend shares the child's live location with a specifically designated secondary guardian. This is a disclosure of highly sensitive personal data to a known, fixed party, creating a privacy threat if the sharing exceeds the child's or primary guardian's expectations, necessity, or authorization scope.
assumptions: Assumes the secondary guardian is a pre-registered recipient rather than an ad hoc audience, and that live location is personal data about the child.

title: Insufficient control over granting and revoking secondary guardian access
description: When the backend grants the secondary guardian access to the child's live location, the data subject or responsible guardian may lack effective means to control who can access the data, for how long, and under what conditions. This creates an unintervenability risk around access management.
assumptions: Assumes the system may not provide granular controls such as time-bounded sharing, easy revocation, or visibility into active access.

title: Potential non-compliance from sharing a child's live location with another guardian
description: Sharing a child's live location with a secondary guardian may trigger heightened legal and regulatory obligations because it involves children's data and precise location data. If the backend grants access without valid authorization, transparency, necessity, or appropriate safeguards, the processing may be non-compliant.
assumptions: Assumes applicable child-privacy, data-protection, or consent/parental-authority requirements apply in the deployment jurisdiction.

title: Sharing analytics with a fixed third-party partner discloses user-derived data to an external party
description: The backend sends aggregated usage and engagement analytics to a predetermined advertising/analytics partner. Even if described as aggregated, the transfer discloses user-derived behavioral information outside the primary service boundary, creating a privacy risk if the aggregation is insufficient, if small cohorts enable singling out, or if the partner can combine the data with other datasets.
assumptions: Assumes the partner is a known, fixed recipient and that the shared analytics are derived from personal data or user behavior rather than being fully anonymous in practice.

title: Partner may further analyze or enrich received analytics beyond what is necessary for app functionality
description: After receiving aggregated usage and engagement analytics, the advertising/analytics partner may perform additional treatment, analysis, enrichment, or profiling for advertising, audience measurement, or cross-service intelligence purposes that are not necessary to deliver the app's core functionality. This can increase disclosure risk and expand the privacy impact beyond the original context of collection.
assumptions: Assumes the partner is permitted or technically able to reuse the received analytics for its own analytics or advertising purposes.

title: Users may lack meaningful control over analytics sharing for ad-funding purposes
description: If the backend shares usage and engagement analytics with an advertising/analytics partner to fund the free tier without granular opt-in/opt-out or audience-specific controls, data subjects may be unable to choose whether, how, or for how long their behavioral data is shared for this secondary purpose.
assumptions: Assumes the app does not provide sufficiently granular controls for third-party analytics/advertising sharing.

title: Third-party analytics sharing may lack adequate privacy risk management
description: Sharing analytics with an external advertising/analytics partner introduces third-party privacy and cybersecurity risk that should be governed through due diligence, contractual restrictions, minimization, aggregation thresholds, retention limits, and re-identification safeguards. If such controls are insufficient, the processing may create non-compliance risk.
assumptions: Assumes the organization may not have fully assessed and managed the privacy/security risks of this partner data-sharing arrangement.
uncertainty_note: This is a governance-oriented threat inferred from the flow context; applicability depends on actual vendor management, contracts, and technical safeguards.

title: SOS/check-in message is attributable to the child
description: The manual check-in / SOS message and attached location are inherently linked to the child sender, creating attributable evidence that the child initiated a specific alert from a specific place and time. This can later be used to prove the child's action, reducing plausible deniability.
assumptions: The backend stores or can reconstruct sender identity, timestamp, and location for the message.

title: Backend may further analyze or enrich precise SOS location beyond what is necessary
description: The backend receives highly sensitive contextual data: a child's SOS/check-in plus current location. If the backend performs additional analytics, profiling, enrichment, or secondary use of this event data beyond routing it to the parent and supporting the emergency feature, it would disclose more about the child than necessary for the stated purpose.
assumptions: The service may log, analyze, correlate, or retain event/location data for purposes beyond immediate delivery of the SOS/check-in.
uncertainty_note: Applies if backend processing goes beyond strictly necessary transmission/storage for the feature; exact backend behavior is not provided.

title: Child may lack control over how SOS/check-in location data is processed
description: When sending a manual check-in / SOS, the child may have limited ability to choose the precision, recipients, retention, or downstream processing of their current location and message. This creates a lack-of-control risk over highly sensitive real-time location disclosure.
assumptions: The app does not offer meaningful controls over granularity, sharing scope, or retention for the SOS/check-in payload.
uncertainty_note: The exact UI/consent controls are not described; threat applies if the child cannot meaningfully configure this flow.

title: Insufficient privacy-aware security controls for child SOS/location transmission
description: This flow carries sensitive child location and emergency-context data. If the backend lacks adequate cybersecurity risk management tailored to privacy risks—such as secure transport handling, access control, minimization in logs, and retention governance—the system may fail to protect this personal data in a compliant manner.
assumptions: Privacy-relevant security controls for this flow may be incomplete or not specifically assessed for child location/emergency data.
uncertainty_note: This is a governance/control threat inferred from the sensitivity of the flow; specific control gaps are not evidenced in the prompt.
